scenes.headline: 8,257 attacks on Europe, explained
scenes.body: ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 · covering all of 2025
scenes.say: European organisations: the EU's cyber agency studied 8,257 incidents. Here is what it found, where the data is thin, and what to do.

scenes.headline: Europe's yearly threat report
scenes.body: Published September 22, 2026 · incidents from January 1 to December 31, 2025 · mostly open sources, plus data shared by EU member states
scenes.say: ENISA, the EU Agency for Cybersecurity, published its Threat Landscape report on September 22. It covers incidents from all of 2025, mostly from public reporting, plus data shared by EU member states.

scenes.headline: of incidents were DDoS attacks
scenes.body: Mostly hacktivist campaigns with little large-scale impact
scenes.say: The most common incident was DDoS, flooding a website until it goes offline. That was 51.3 percent of incidents, mostly hacktivist campaigns with little large-scale impact.

scenes.headline: of money-driven attacks were ransomware
scenes.body: Financially motivated activity: 29.3% of incidents, and the most impactful threat in the short term
scenes.say: But the damage comes from criminals chasing money. Ransomware made up 47.3 percent of financially motivated activity, which ENISA calls the most impactful threat in the short term.

scenes.headline: Mostly through unpatched holes
scenes.body: Where the entry route was known: 60.4% exploited a vulnerability · 20.7% misconfiguration or accidental exposure
scenes.say: How did attackers get in? Where the entry route was known, 60.4 percent exploited a vulnerability, and 20.7 percent came from misconfiguration or accidental exposure.

scenes.headline: That rests on a thin slice
scenes.body: Only 5.2% of unauthorised-access incidents had an identifiable entry route
scenes.say: Here is the limit. Only 5.2 percent of those break-ins had a known entry route, so that figure rests on a thin slice of the data.

scenes.headline: Public administration topped the list
scenes.body: 31.8% of incidents · most of them DDoS
scenes.say: Public administration was the most targeted sector, with 31.8 percent of incidents, most of them DDoS.

scenes.headline: AI boosts skills, no breakthrough yet
scenes.body: Attackers mostly used off-the-shelf AI tools · ENISA expects more attack stages to be AI-enabled in 2026
scenes.say: What about AI? Attackers mostly used off-the-shelf AI tools to boost the skills they already had, not for breakthroughs. But ENISA expects more stages of an attack to be AI-enabled in 2026.

scenes.headline: What the numbers can't show
scenes.body: Based largely on public reporting · espionage often surfaces months or years later · many attacker claims could not be verified
scenes.say: Read it with care. The data leans on public reporting, spying often comes to light months or years later, and many attacker claims could not be verified.

scenes.headline: Loud attacks get counted. Quiet ones do damage.
scenes.body: DDoS fills the charts, but unpatched systems and ransomware are where the losses are.
scenes.say: Analyst note: loud attacks get counted, quiet ones do the damage. DDoS fills the charts, but unpatched systems and ransomware are where the real losses are.

scenes.headline: What to do this month
items: Check for misconfigured or exposed services
Have a DDoS plan for public websites
Keep offline backups and test a restore
scenes.say: What to do this month. Patch your internet-facing systems first. Check for misconfigured or exposed services. Have a plan for DDoS on your public websites. And keep offline backups, then test a restore.
